newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba sugar harvest starts, officials see increase.
newsitem.headline: Cuba sugar harvest starts, officials see increase.

text.p: Cuba's 1996-97 sugar cane harvest has begun and Sugar Minister Nelson Torres said Tuesday he expected production to be more than last year's 4.45 million tonnes.
State media said milling began at the Luis Enrique Carracedo mill in eastern Granma province Sunday night. Other mills in eastern areas are expected to start up in the coming days.
Torres, attending a conference on sugar in Havana, told reporters the harvest would be an improvement on last year's crop.

He declined to give a precise target, but said that the increase would not be as much as one million tonnes over last year. Replying to questions about some unofficial estimates the harvest will be around 5.3 million tonnes, he said production would probably not be this much.
Torres was speaking during a forum in Havana on investment in sugar cane and related industries in Latin America and the Caribbean.
He said that of the country's 156 mills, 149 would operate during the harvest, expected to last until April. Of these, 36 mills would be operating by the end of this month, he said.

Cuban authorities invariably want the harvest to be as rapid as possible, partly because after April yields from cane fall off rapidly. But in recent years the harvest has tended to drag on until June.

Last year's crop, while low by the standards of the 1980s when Cuba regularly achieved crops in excess of seven million tonnes, marked the end of a steep decline in the island's main export since the collapse of Cuba's old economic ally the former Soviet Union. Production the previous year, 1994-95, was just 3.3 million tonnes.
Also attending the sugar forum, Peter Baron, director of the International Sugar Organisation, told reporters that he believed Cuba's sugar crop could be around 4.8 million to five million tonnes.

On financing for the crop, Torres said the island had secured foreign credits for all of the 13 sugar producing provinces. He said in reply to a question that the total sum involved in financing was slightly more than $320 million.

Torres did not give details of the financing, secured from a series of foreign banks and trading houses. The improvement in last year's harvest was partly attributed to credits secured towards input such as fertilisers that had been scarce since the early 1990s.

Authorities were concerned last month by damage to cane caused by Hurricane Lili that swept over western and central parts of the island on October 17-18. But they have since said that although areas of cane were flattened or flooded, most of this cane would still be useable.
